title: NEOVASCULAR GLAUCOMA (NVG): A Comprehensive Guide
summary: Neovascular glaucoma is a challenging condition driven by posterior segment ischaemia, leading to the formation of a fibrovascular membrane in the iris and drainage angle. This guide details the progression from open-angle to synechial closure, common causes like CrVO and diabetes, and the transformative role of anti-VEGF therapies.

sections.title: Pathophysiology & Progression
content: 1. Posterior segment ischaemia drives neovascularization of the iris and drainage angle.
2. This leads to the development of a fibrovascular membrane.
3. Initially, the membrane overlies the trabecular meshwork so that the angle appears open.
4. Over time, Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS) form.
5. The fibrovascular membrane contracts to cause complete synechial angle closure.

sections.title: Key Causes & Risk Factors
content: Ischaemic CrVO (common); risk of progression to NVG is 50%.
Diabetic retinopathy (common); risk of NVG highest in PDr.
Other vascular disorders: OIS, CrAO, BrVO.
Other retinal disease: chronic retinal detachment, sickle cell retinopathy.
Retinal or choroidal tumours.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Presentation
content: Pain is often a feature and may be severe.
The predisposing condition may be known or suggested by history (e.g. sudden loss of vision several months previously in cases of CrVO and NVG).
Iris rubeosis: abnormal/non-radial vessels at pupil sphincter margin.
Increased Intraocular Pressure (iIOP).
AC flare/cells and hyphaema.
Ectropion uvea.
Conjunctival injection and corneal oedema (if acute iIOP or decompensating).
Disc changes and field loss as for POAG (see E Primary open-angle glaucoma, pp. 390–1).

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations
content: Dilated fundoscopy in all cases ± FFA to determine cause.
Carotid Doppler US: performed if no retinal pathology or asymmetric diabetic retinopathy is found.
B-scan US: if there is a poor fundal view (cataract may be associated with chronic retinal pathology such as tumours, detachment, and inflammation).
Haematological/biochemical factors: looking for factors that increase the hypoxic drive, e.g. anaemia.

sections.title: Core Treatment Philosophy
sections.content: Treatment of NVG (see p. 405) has often been challenging and unsatisfactory but is undergoing a positive transformation with the advent of anti-VeGF therapies. It is important to remember that anti-VeGF therapy alone will not control NVG, unless the posterior segment hypoxic drive is also addressed through adequate PrP, etc.

sections.title: Managing Neovascularization
content: PrP to decrease retinal ischaemic drive long term.
If no fundal view exists, anti-VeGF therapy can be administered to temporize.
Vitrectomy/endolaser photocoagulation ± cataract extraction (depending on visual prognosis).
Anti-VeGF impact: Significant impact on neovascularization and improves survival of drainage surgery.
Bevacizumab Evidence: Small retrospective studies show regression of neovascularization and decreased IOP when used alone or with PrP.

sections.title: Managing IOP and Inflammation
content: Cycloplegic: e.g. atropine 1% 2×/d.
Frequent topical steroids: e.g. prednisolone acetate 1% 1- to 4-hourly.
Ocular hypotensive agents: as for POAG.
If medical treatment fails: Consider trabeculectomy (augmented), tubeshunt procedures, or cyclodestruction (e.g. cyclodiode), depending on visual prognosis.

sections.title: Pain Management & The Blind Eye
content: Use Cycloplegia (atropine) and topical corticosteroids for pain.
Lubricants for sick corneal epithelium (keep high index of suspicion for microbial keratitis).
Consider full ocular surface regime for dry eyes/blepharitis/drop toxicity.
If the eye is blind and painful: Consider retrobulbar alcohol or chlorpromazine, or evisceration/enucleation.
